title: Command substitution: $( )
summary: Put a command's output inside another command: dates, counts, paths, passwords in scripts.

text: $( ) runs the command inside it first, then puts what it printed in its place.
- The outer command never sees $(date +%A): it only gets Monday.
- This is called command substitution. Nested ones run from the inside out.
Backticks ` ` do the same job. You meet them in old scripts and answers online: recognise them.
- Write $( ): it nests without backslashes, and ` is easy to mix up with '.
- Both lines above print the same thing: the first one is much easier to read.
Without quotes, the shell cuts the output at each space, and expands any * in it.
- The quotes inside start fresh: "$(dirname "$f")" is correct.
- In x=$(cmd) nothing is cut, but the quotes never hurt.
The newlines at the end of the output are removed. That is why the value fits in a sentence or a test.
- Newlines in the middle stay: $(ls) keeps one name per line, inside quotes.
- wc -l < file prints only the number; wc -l file adds the name.
x=$(cmd) keeps cmd's exit code, so if, || and set -e see the failure.
- Inside another command's arguments, only that command's code counts: echo succeeds, the failure is lost.
- So store the output first, check it, then use it.

scheme: tool --password "$(pass show db)"   ✘ ps shows it
text: In a script, $(pass show db) reads the password when the script runs: the file never holds it, so it can go into git.
- Keep it in a variable. A command's arguments can be read by every user of the machine with ps, while it runs.
- pass prints the password on the first line. If the entry holds more lines, keep only that one: $(pass show db | head -n 1).
